newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel pullout plan faces crossfire of condemnation.
newsitem.headline: Israel pullout plan faces crossfire of condemnation.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu turned up the heat on Friday in his defence of a further West Bank troop pullout, target of a crossfire of condemnation by Israeli hardliners and PLO leaders.

Palestinians charged Israel was killing the peace process in its decision to hand over an additional fraction of the West Bank. The scope of the pullout -- decreed by Israel without negotiation with the Palestinians -- was denounced by the PLO as insufficient and in violation of peace accords.

A number of hawks threatened to bolt Netanyahu's coalition over the move, approved by a narrow 10-7 margin in an overnight cabinet session. Netanyahu answered with a veiled threat to seek other, more moderate partners if his government were shaken.
Speaking to Israel's Channel Two Television Netanyahu defended the pullout as a balance "between guarding our assets and progress in a process which is crucial for our future".
Under the cabinet decision two percent of the West Bank -- land now under full Israeli control -- would be handed over along with seven percent now under joint Israel-PLO rule.
Israel already handed three percent of the West Bank to the PLO since a 1993 peace deal, including eight major Arab towns.

In a news conference, Netanyahu said of rightist opponents, "Maybe there are people who want to blow up the (peace) process" but he said he had stood up to Palestinians and Israeli doves who pressed for pulling out of 30 percent of the West Bank.
Israel's key ally Washington has endorsed the Israeli proposal. Palestinians vehemently oppose it.
"What the Israeli government has done with its decision is kill this (peace) process," said senior PLO official Ahmed Korei, who negotiated the broad 1993 peace deal with Israel.
Asked by Israel Radio if he backed halting the talks, Korei said "Without any doubt."
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat condemned the decision to reporters in Gaza: "This is a big deceit operation. It came from one party, without consultation with us."

Addressing the threat by eight members of his coalition to bolt over the pullback, Netanyahu fired off a warning of his own, raising the spectre of a "national-unity" government with the centre-left Labour party:
"I hope these comrades will not force me to consider other possibilities, of forming governments," Netanyahu said.
Arafat aide Tayeb Abdel-Rahim said an official Palestinian response would be decided later on Friday.
He said the PLO in a U.S.-brokered accord sealed in January on the three further Israeli West Bank withdrawals understood each would be 30 percent of the land now in Israeli hands.
Israel says the scope of the pullbacks are solely up to it.
The PLO was already enraged at Israel's decision last month to build a new settlement of 6,500 homes in Arab East Jerusalem.

Thousands of Palestinians accompanied by Israeli leftists prayed for peace at a West Bank protest on Friday against the settlement decision. The protesters were closely watched by Israeli soldiers in battle gear, backed by snipers and at least one machinegun. The demonstration ended peacefully.

In a separate incident, Palestinian youths hurled stones at Israeli troops and vehicles in the West Bank village of Beit Ummar, believed to be included in the further redeployment. The troops fired tear gas in response. No injuries were reported.

The Israeli decision on the withdrawal came hours before Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak left Cairo on his way to Washington, the latest Middle East leader to discuss the troubled peace process with U.S. President Bill Clinton.
The U.S. State Department welcomed the new withdrawal as a "demonstration of Israel's commitment to the peace process," but added it hoped for more in the next stages of withdrawal.

Israel said the pullback would take at least 48 hours. It must complete the third phase of redeployment by mid-1998. Final borders are to be decided in permanent status talks set to begin this month where Jerusalem is also to be negotiated.
Netanyahu's government commands 66 of the 120 seats in parliament. Rightist disenchantment has increased since the January handover of most of the West Bank town of Hebron.
